case_name: Kirschbaum v. Our Voices Publishing Co. et. al.
text:
Kirschbaum v. "Our Voices" Publishing Co. et. al.

[1972] 1 O.R. 737-739

ONTARIO

[HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE]

HAINES, J.

22nd NOVEMBER 1971.

Practice -- Discovery -- Libel action -- Correspondence between solicitors -- Privilege -- Rule 326.
Discovery of correspondence passing between solicitors may be allowed where relevant.  In a libel action where conduct up to verdict is relevant, discovery should be permitted of correspondence passing between solicitors which the trial Judge may allow to go to the jury in whole or in part as admissions of fact as to malice or motive or aggravation of damages and not as hypothetical admissions for the purpose of settlement only.
APPEAL from an order of the Senior Master refusing to direct the defendants to reattend and answer questions pertaining to correspondence passing between the solicitors for the parties.

R.N. Starr, Q.C., for applicant.
J.H. Porter, for respondent.

HAINES, J.:-- This is an appeal from the order of the Senior
Master dated November 5, 1971, refusing to direct the
defendants to reattend and answer questions pertaining to a
series of letters passing between the solicitors for the
parties commencing on October 1, 1963, and concluding on July
24, 1964.  The action is for $250,000 damages for libel arising
out of a lengthy newspaper article published by the defendants.
The plaintiff contends the words were meant and were understood
to mean that the plaintiff gave instructions on how to kill
Slovakian Jews without killing them himself, that he had the
same power and responsibility on domestic affairs in Slovakia
as did Hilter in Nazi Germany, and that he was in Slovakia the
type of man that Hilter was in Nazi Germany.  The defendants
plead the statements of fact are true, and in so far as they
consist of expressions of opinion are fair comment made in good
faith and without malice on a matter of public interest.

Being a libel action, the conduct of the defendants from the
publication of the libel to the very moment of the verdict may
be considered by the jury:  see Gatley on Libel and Slander,
6th ed., p. 1258.  I think it is beyond argument that if there
were no questions of the correspondence being without prejudice
that the correspondence would be evidence of a refusal to
apologize, of malice and motive and aggravation of damages.

The learned Senior Master held that since the first letter
was written "without prejudice" that it and the succeeding
letters were without prejudice and could not be the subject of
discovery, although only the first letter bore that term.  I
have read the letters carefully and at least two things become
apparent.  First, settlement was at times in the minds of the
parties.  Second, the plaintiff's solicitor was with skill, and
if I may say so with prejudice, developing his case so as to
secure a definite refusal to apologize and obtain evidence to
show malice, motive and aggravation of damages.

The question then arises whether the correspondence conducted
in this manner between two solicitors knowledgeable in the law
makes part or all of the correspondence admissible in evidence
at the trial.  It is axiomatic in our law of evidence that any
fact rationally probative of a material proposition is
admissible unless it is shown to be obnoxious to an
exclusionary rule.  But of equal importance, and frequently
overlooked in examing the exclusionary rules, is the rule of
multiple or alternative admissibility. Evidence which is
inadmissible through one gateway of admission may be perfectly
admissible through another gateway.  The cases are collected in
7 C.E.D. (Ont. 2nd), pp. 16-9.

Correspondence without prejudice is one of the exclusionary
rules.  Contrary to popular belief in some quarters that the
shibboleth "without prejudice" written on a letter protects it
from subsequent use as an admission is not accurate:  see 4
Wigmore, 2nd ed., paras. 1060-2.  That learned authority points
out that the basis of the exclusion is a hypothetical admission
or concession for the purpose of securing peace or settlement;
and since it does not represent the parties' true belief it
cannot be taken as a true admission.  Therefore, the question
to be considered is, what was the view and intention of the
party in making the admission; whether it was to concede a fact
hypothetically, in order to effect a settlement, or to declare
a fact really to exist.  At this stage the rules of alternative
admissibility become especially worthy of consideration,
because the declaration as to the existence of the fact may
make it admissible on a variety of issues.  Williston and Rolls
in their work on Civil Procedure, c. 16, mention several where
so-called without prejudice correspondence is admissible, such
as (a) where it results in settlement (b) is not a genuine
attempt at settlement but a repudiation (c) in actions for
reformation (d) it contains notice of an act of bankruptcy (e)
to disprove laches or to prove waiver or election (f) its main
purpose is to threaten or malign.  Wigmore adds several sundry
instances.

In my opinion there is sufficient within the correspondence
in question which a trial Judge may allow to go to the jury in
whole or in part, as admissions of fact, as to malice or motive
or aggravation of damages.  To he will do after hearing the
evidence and argument in the absence of the jury.

That being so, it is my opinion that the parties should have
discovery on this correspondence so that in the preparatory
stage the parties may explore the facts and circumstances
surrounding the correspondence and discover whether the
admissions were hypothetical or a statement of facts intended
to represent the real position of the litigant.  To do
otherwise may preclude the trial Judge from having all relevant
facts developed and placed before him.

No fear need arise that once having obtained an answer on
discovery the opposite party has an absolute right to read it
to the jury.  The common law, the Evidence Act, R.S.O. 1970, c.
151, and the Rules of Practice repose in the trial Judge the
necessary discretion to admit or reject such statements.

The appeal will be allowed with costs.

Appeal allowed.
